exposure: contact with baby after childbirth (skin-to-skin, rooming-in)
introduction of traditional foods and medicine
outcome: infant feeding practices (breastfeeding initiation, exclusive breastfeeding duration, timing of solid food introduction, timing of traditional food introduction)
reported challenges and positive experiences with breastfeeding
cohort: The study included 145 self-identifying Indigenous women of childbearing age (15-49 years) who had delivered in the past three years in three Northwest Territories (NWT) communities.
finding: The study found high rates of breastfeeding intention (73%) and initiation (87%) among Indigenous mothers, with 44% exclusively breastfeeding for up to three months and 50% introducing solid foods between six and twelve months.
mod_finding: Rates of skin-to-skin contact and rooming-in were significantly higher among participants who had vaginal births compared to those who had emergency and scheduled Caesarean sections.
cross-section timing: Data was collected from mothers at a single point in time, with participants having delivered within the past three years prior to data collection, reporting on practices up to 12 months of infant age.
